name: Portulaca oleracea
lead: Portulaca oleracea, commonly purslane, is a warm-climate succulent annual eaten as a leafy vegetable in the Mediterranean, Middle East, Asia and Mexico and used in folk medicine in many countries.[1][2] For appearance, it enters the picture in two ways: as a soothing botanical in skincare, where one DailyMed-listed essence combines Portulaca oleracea extract with niacinamide, glycerin and lotus flower extract, and as a food rich in omega-3 alpha-linolenic acid and vitamin E that people include in diets aimed at skin and overall health.[3][1][6]

Laboratory research describes anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and wound-healing activity. A 2015 review catalogued its flavonoids, alkaloids and fatty acids and their reported pharmacological effects, and a mouse study reported faster excision-wound closure with a crude topical preparation.[4][5] A randomized trial of an oral purslane extract for chronic hand eczema is the closest human skin study. No controlled clinical trial of topical purslane for skin appearance was found.

sections.h: How it is used for appearance
paras: In cosmetics, purslane extract is promoted as a soothing botanical, often in essences, toners and creams marketed for sensitive or irritated skin, where the claimed route is calming redness by way of anti-inflammatory plant compounds.[3][4] The listed essence pairs it with niacinamide and glycerin, the humectant and tone-evening ingredients common in routine-style skincare.[3]

As a food, purslane supplies alpha-linolenic acid and vitamin E, nutrients that proponents link with skin condition and general health; Grokipedia reports figures such as 12.2 mg of vitamin E per 100 g raw leaves, higher than many common greens.[2][6] Pigmented betalains in the plant are described as a stress-response photoprotective pigment in the plant itself.[2]

The plant is a prostrate, fleshy herb with reddish stems and small yellow flowers, and is a weed in many regions.[1][2] It is eaten fresh in salads and cooked in soups, and seeds have been ground into flour.[2] Its leaves are rich in alpha-linolenic acid, an omega-3 fatty acid, and in vitamin E, but are also very high in oxalates.[1][6]

Traditional medicine has used purslane as an anti-inflammatory, diuretic and for burns and fevers, and Chinese tradition calls it a vegetable for long life.[2][4] Grokipedia says the World Health Organization has called it a 'global panacea'.[2] Persian medicine uses it for skin ailments, according to the authors of a hand-eczema trial.[11]

A review of its phytochemistry and pharmacology summarised reported antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, wound-healing and other effects, mostly from cell and animal work.[4] A 2000 study reported analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects in animals, and a 2003 study in mice reported that a crude extract accelerated wound contraction.[5][7] A study of wild Nepalese vegetables measured antioxidant capacity of purslane extracts in chemical assays.[8]

Beyond skin, systematic reviews and trials have examined purslane for blood sugar control, where a meta-analysis of randomized trials reported a significant reduction in fasting glucose but no significant change in insulin or insulin resistance measures, and for musculoskeletal conditions, where a 2025 review of 69 studies including 9 clinical trials described reductions in inflammatory cytokines.[12][13]

Purslane is high in oxalates, which is relevant to dietary intake.[1] The product label for the essence advises external use only, avoiding broken or irritated skin, and stopping use if irritation or rash occurs.[3]

A 2024 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 70 adults with mild to moderate chronic hand eczema compared an oral standardized purslane preparation with placebo, both with topical Vaseline, over four weeks. Physician-reported fissure scores were significantly lower in the purslane group among those analysed.[11]

No clinical studies of purslane for skin appearance were found. A registered phase 2 trial examined purslane for oral lichen planus, and another registered study of an eyelash serum listed purslane among its ingredients.[9][10] Results have not been published.

card.summary: Edible succulent weed used as a soothing skincare botanical, backed by lab and animal data but no skin-appearance trials.
card.note: Evidence is from lab and animal studies; no topical human appearance trials found.

quick.overview:
Purslane is a common edible succulent used in folk medicine, now added to K-beauty-style soothing products.

Research reports anti-inflammatory and wound-healing effects in cells and animals. No clinical trials of topical use for appearance were found.
quick.mechanism: Flavonoids, alkaloids and fatty acids in the plant show antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity in laboratory assays.
quick.risks: Leaves are high in oxalates when eaten. Topical product labels advise avoiding broken skin and stopping use if irritation occurs.
